title: Why Do Your Fingers Wrinkle in Water?
description:
Your fingers don't prune just because skin soaks up water. If the nerve to a finger is cut, it stays smooth.
Here's how your nervous system makes the wrinkles, and why scientists still argue about what they're for.

subtitles: Why do your fingers wrinkle in water?
Stay in a warm bath for a while, and your fingertips turn into little prunes.
Your arms don't do it.
Your back doesn't do it.
Only the skin of your hands and feet, most of all your fingertips and toes.
Most people think the answer is simple.
The skin soaks up water, swells, and folds.
That is part of the story.
But it leaves out the strangest part.
If the nerve to a finger is cut, that finger stays smooth.
Soak it as long as you like.
By the end of this video, you will know why your nervous system decides whether you wrinkle.
And why scientists still argue about what it is for.
Start with the simple idea, because it is not wrong.
The outer layer of your skin is a sheet of dead, flattened cells.
They are packed with proteins that hold on to water.
In a bath, that layer takes in water and swells a little.
Wet a sheet of paper on one side and you see the same thing.
The wet side grows, the dry side does not, and the sheet curls.
Picture a carpet that is slightly too big for its room.
It can't spread out, so it buckles.
A soaked outer layer, glued to the tissue beneath it, gets pushed the same way.
If swelling were the whole answer, though, a finger would wrinkle whether or not its nerves worked.
It doesn't.
The big clue came from hospitals.
In the 1930s, two doctors, Thomas Lewis and George Pickering, studied patients.
Each had a damaged nerve in the arm.
In water, the fingers served by that nerve did not wrinkle.
The healthy fingers next to them did.
Same skin.
Same water.
Same time in the bath.
The only difference was the nerve.
Later work narrowed it down to the nerves that run on autopilot.
The ones that control sweating and blood flow, without you thinking about it.
So wrinkling is not just something water does to skin.
It is something your body does.
Here is how it seems to work.
Your fingertips are covered in sweat pores.
Water seeps in through them, into the skin.
That water probably upsets the balance of salts around tiny nerve endings, and the nerves respond.
They signal the small blood vessels under the fingertip to narrow.
Less blood flows in.
The soft pad of the fingertip loses a little volume.
None of this is instant.
In warm water, it takes several minutes before the wrinkles show.
Now the skin on top has too much surface for what is underneath.
And it is anchored down at many points.
So it gets pulled in between those anchors.
Ridges rise, valleys sink.
Computer models of fingertips found that either effect alone needs a lot to make wrinkles.
Swelling on top, shrinking below, together make them easily.
But why only hands and feet?
The palms and soles have more sweat pores than any other skin on your body.
They also have a dense mesh of nerves and blood vessels.
That is the hardware this reflex needs.
Most other skin does not have it in the same way.
Toes have it too, which is why they prune along with your fingers.
Doctors have even used the bath as a test.
If a finger does not wrinkle, it can be a sign that its nerves are not working properly.
And one small study, with just 3 people, found something else.
The same finger made the same pattern of wrinkles when it was soaked again a day later.
That suggests the blood vessels underneath set the map.
And when you get out and dry off, the blood flow returns and the pad fills back up.
Within about half an hour, the wrinkles are gone.
So why would your body bother?
If wrinkling is controlled by nerves, it might be there for a reason.
One idea is that wrinkled fingertips work like tyre treads.
Think about where our ancestors needed grip most.
Wet rocks by a river, slippery branches after rain, wet food in their hands.
On a car tyre, the grooves give water somewhere to go, so the rubber can grip the road.
Wrinkles might do the same thing, draining water away so your fingers can grip wet things.
In 2013, a team at Newcastle University tested it.
People moved wet marbles from one box to another.
With wrinkled fingers, they were faster.
But in 2014, a team in Berlin ran a similar test with 40 people.
They found no advantage at all.
So the honest answer is: we don't know yet.
The how is fairly clear.
The why is still open.
Whatever the reason, the reflex itself is real.
You can watch it switch on in a few minutes in warm water.
So, why do your fingers wrinkle in water?
Water soaks into the outer layer of your skin, and it swells.
But the real trigger is your nervous system.
It tightens the blood vessels in your fingertips, and the pad shrinks.
The skin above it folds into a pattern.
Cut the nerve, and the fingers stay smooth.
It is not your skin giving up in the bath.
It is your body making a change.
Here is a question for you.
If wrinkles really help us grip, why do our fingers not stay wrinkled all the time?
Tell me what you think in the comments.
